verdict.reason:
I checked every claim against the code and they hold.
- **The query:** `events_that_overlap_query` (calendar.rs:94-101) filters with `COALESCE(NULLIF(end_datetime,''), start_datetime) >= ?2`. The column is `end_datetime TEXT NOT NULL`, the COALESCE result has no affinity, and the bound value is plain text, so SQLite compares the raw text byte by byte.
- **What the callers pass:** all three bind `?2` as `from.format("%Y-%m-%dT00:00:00Z")`: managers.rs:1663-1666, wx_app.rs:13599-13602 and wx_app.rs:15551-15555.
- **What gets stored:** both ways an event is saved here write a space between date and time. `event_entry` (managers.rs:2225-2241, used for new events at managers.rs:1598 and for edits) and `store_new_item` (managers.rs:4073-4114) both write `"{date} {time}"`, or the bare date for an all-day event. The date comes from `as_stored_date` (`YYYY-MM-DD`) and the time from `as_stored_time` (`HH:MM`) in wx_item_form.rs:2002 and 2146. `save_calendar_event` stores the strings unchanged.
- **The comparison fails:** `'2026-10-12 10:00' >= '2026-10-12T00:00:00Z'` is false because a space (0x20) sorts before 'T' (0x54). A bare `'2026-11-01'` is a prefix of the bound, so it sorts lower too.
- **The dates in the example:** weeks start on Monday (`THE_WEEK_STARTS_ON`, ui_types.rs:1293), and 2026-10-12 is a Monday. `window()` gives the first day of the week or month (ui_types.rs:1350-1362).
- **Nothing puts it back:** `falls_on` returns a one-off event as it is, so only what the SQL returns gets drawn. The reload after saving reads the database again instead of patching the list in memory (managers.rs:1653-1672). A newly made one-off event on the first day therefore disappears the moment it is saved.
- **The code already knows the formats differ:** the comment at ui_types.rs:1793-1797 says "the editor writes a space ... every sync writes a T, and a space sorts before a T". It fixed the sort and never the query.
- **No test catches it:** the window tests at calendar.rs:1317-1400 and the three integration tests use only `T...Z` strings or repeating series, which a second query returns anyway.
- **Not already recorded:** nothing in .planning/WINDOWS.md covers this.

The finding needs two corrections:
- **Repeating events are not affected.** `repeating_events_query` returns every series whatever its dates, so only one-off events go missing. That is still the common case.
- **The fix is larger than it needs to be.** The upper bound already works for every stored shape: `'2026-10-18 09:00'` and `'2026-10-18'` both sort at or below `'2026-10-18T23:59:59Z'`. So `to` and the `<=` can stay as they are.

The alerts path (wx_app.rs:13599) has the same flaw on its first day, which is yesterday, so it matters little there.

It belongs in `must` because a calendar meant for screen reader users silently leaves out events the person just made, on the day the week or month view opens on.
verdict.corrected_problem: The window's lower bound compares raw text: `COALESCE(NULLIF(end_datetime,''), start_datetime) >= ?2`, with ?2 bound as 'YYYY-MM-DDT00:00:00Z' by all three callers. Events made or edited here are stored as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM', or as a bare 'YYYY-MM-DD' when all-day (managers.rs event_entry and store_new_item). A space sorts before 'T', and a bare date is a prefix of the bound, so a one-off local event that ends on the window's first day compares as earlier than the window and is never fetched. Repeating events come back through the separate series query and are not affected. The upper bound `start_datetime <= 'YYYY-MM-DDT23:59:59Z'` already admits every stored shape.
verdict.corrected_fix: Change only the lower bound, in one place. In `events_that_could_fall_between`, bind the date part of `from` for ?2: `from.get(..10).unwrap_or(from)`. Any value that ends on that day or later is then >= it, whichever shape it was stored in. Leave `to` and the `<=` as they are. First add a red test in calendar.rs: store a one-off event as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM' and a one-day all-day event as a bare 'YYYY-MM-DD', both on the window's first day, then assert both come back from `events_that_could_fall_between(acct, "<that day>T00:00:00Z", ...)`.

all.title: Waiting moves and deletes are replayed by UID without the folder's UIDVALIDITY
all.location: src/data/message_cache/moves_waiting.rs:217-274 (keep_a_move_waiting) and mod.rs:2343-2351 (moves_waiting schema); src/application/moves_waiting.rs:626-645 (replay_one); mod.rs:2313-2322 (waiting_flag_changes, same shape)
all.what_this_is: A move or delete made while the server cannot be reached is kept as a waiting row (account, folder path, uid). Every check replays it first, as step 2 of the IMAP sequence, before any folder is synced.
all.problem: An IMAP UID names a message only within one UIDVALIDITY. The waiting row does not record the UIDVALIDITY, and replay_one sends `move_it/delete_it(from, waiting.uid, ...)` with no check. The renumbering that forget_folder_messages handles (messages.rs:2186-2203) is noticed only during the folder sync, which runs after the replay.
all.concrete_case: Offline, the person deletes message M (uid 42) in Trash. That is DeleteOutright, kept waiting. Before the next check, the server renumbers Trash, for example after a server migration or after the folder is deleted and recreated elsewhere. Some other message now holds uid 42. The check replays DeleteOutright 42 and expunges that other message permanently. A waiting Move would move the wrong message in the same way.
all.fix: Add a nullable uid_validity column to moves_waiting (and to waiting_flag_changes) and fill it from folders.uid_validity when the row is kept. In replay_one, compare it with the UIDVALIDITY the SELECT reports. On a mismatch, do not send by UID: fall back to the Message-ID lookup the module already has (where_it_is, application/moves_waiting.rs:909), or put the change back.
all.if_skipped: This is rare, but when it happens it permanently deletes or moves a message the person never touched.
all.ledger_entry: new; ledger rows on renumbering (69) concern the sync, not the queues

verdict.reason: I read the code and the finding holds. `keep_a_move_waiting` (data/message_cache/moves_waiting.rs:217-274) stores only the folder path and the uid, and the `moves_waiting` table (mod.rs:2343-2351) has no UIDVALIDITY column. `replay_one` (application/moves_waiting.rs:621-645) first sends the marks by that uid and then calls `move_it`, `delete_it` or `copy_it` with `waiting.uid`. The `MailController` methods behind them (mail_controller.rs:696-728) SELECT the folder only when it is not already selected, and they throw away the `MailboxStatus`, so the UIDVALIDITY the server reports is never compared with anything. `ImapSession::delete_message` with no trash path sets \Deleted and then runs `UID EXPUNGE {uid}` (imap.rs:1648-1693), which is permanent. Renumbering is noticed in one place only, inside the folder sync (mail_sync.rs:1742-1766), and `set_folder_uid_validity` is called only from there. The sync runs after `replay_the_moves_that_were_waiting` (wx_app.rs:18346), as the comment at mail_sync.rs:1834-1847 says. The menu's own background send and a rule's or an emptied Trash's delete at a check (`delete_here_then_at_the_server`, :834-856) also go through `replay_one`, so the gap is not limited to offline use. It also covers a renumbering that happened between the last sync and the person's action. The flag queue sends by uid in the same way (wx_app.rs:18465-18473), but a wrong mark is far less serious. A crossing removes the message at the source by uid too (mail_across_accounts.rs:672). If the uid is not in the folder at all, the server answers OK and nothing happens, so that half does no harm. The harmful half is that after a renumbering uid 42 can belong to a different message, and that message is expunged or moved. Nothing in WINDOWS.md covers it: ledger 52, on row 69, is about the renumbering announcement, and Research-1 row 52 is about seeing a real renumbering at all. It is rare, a real server has to change UIDVALIDITY, and Gmail almost never does. When it does happen, a message the person never touched is lost for good, so it belongs in should rather than must.
verdict.corrected_problem: A waiting move, delete or copy is sent by UID with no check that the folder still uses the numbering that UID came from. `replay_one` sends the marks and the command by `waiting.uid`, and the controller discards the UIDVALIDITY that its SELECT reports. It skips the SELECT entirely when the folder is already selected. A renumbering is only noticed later, in the folder sync. If the server changed UIDVALIDITY after the last sync, whether before or after the person acted, a waiting DeleteOutright expunges whichever message now holds that uid, and a Move, DeleteToTrash or crossing moves it. The same path is used by the menu's immediate background send and by rule and empty-Trash deletes. The flag queue has the same shape with lower stakes.
verdict.corrected_fix: Add a nullable `uid_validity` column to `moves_waiting` with `ensure_column_exists`, filled from `folders.uid_validity` for the source folder when the row is first kept. A row that already exists keeps its original value, the same way it keeps `from` and `uid`. Add a method to `ReplaysAMove` that returns the source folder's current UIDVALIDITY, either from STATUS or by having the session remember the value from its last SELECT. Today nothing surfaces that value to the replay. In `replay_one`, compare the two before `send_the_marks_first`. If they differ, look up the message's Message-ID in the source folder with the existing `where_it_is`. With exactly one match, send by that uid. With none or several, treat it as Refused so the change is put back, and the next sync re-reads the renumbered folder anyway. A NULL value on an upgraded row skips the check. Write the red test first: a loopback server that reports a different UIDVALIDITY, holding another message at the old uid, which must survive the replay. Give the crossing's `remove_at_the_source` the same check. The flag queue can take the same column later as a nice-to-have.

all.title: Outbox rows are never claimed, so Undo Send can say 'taken back' while the send loop sends the message
all.location: src/data/message_cache/outbox.rs:122-133 (outbox_messages_that_may_go_now), 392-398 (delete_outbox_message); src/presentation/wx_app.rs:24590, 24701 (flush), 24323-24353 (Undo Send)
all.what_this_is: The flush reads the rows that may go, then sends each one and deletes it afterwards. Undo Send saves a draft, then deletes the row, and uses `true` from that delete as its proof that it caught the message.
all.problem: Reading a row does not claim it. outbox.rs:386-391 says 'taken back' about a message that has gone is the one answer this must never give. But a delete that returns true proves only that the row was still there, not that no flush is holding it in memory. The same missing claim causes lead A's double send.
all.concrete_case: A message is held until 09:00:10. At 09:00:09.99 the person presses Undo Send. what_undo_send_takes_back still sees the message as held, and the draft is saved. Meanwhile the one-second tick sees the moment arrive and the flush reads the row. Undo's delete then returns true, the composer opens with the draft, and 'taken back' is announced. The flush still holds the row and sends it.
all.fix: Add a nullable sending_since column (an additive change) and claim each row before sending with `UPDATE outbox_queue SET sending_since = ?now WHERE id = ?1 AND sending_since IS NULL`. Skip the row when 0 rows change. Change Undo's delete to `... AND sending_since IS NULL`, clear the claim on a failed send, and release claims older than a few minutes when the program starts. This one change also closes lead A.
all.if_skipped: In a narrow window someone is told a message was stopped when it went, which the code calls the one unacceptable answer.
all.ledger_entry: extends the mapper's lead A (not in the ledger)

verdict.reason:
The lines say what the finding claims, and the race can really happen, but the concrete case as written cannot. outbox_messages_that_may_go_now (outbox.rs:122-133) only reads rows. flush_outbox (wx_app.rs:24587-24603) takes its `now` and reads the queue inside an rt.spawn task, after MessageCache::new has opened the database and run its migrations. It deletes a row only after the SMTP send finishes (24701), and it only checks that delete for Err, so an Ok(false) passes silently. undo_send (24263-24353) checks readiness against Local::now(), saves a draft, and then trusts a bare `DELETE ... WHERE id` returning true. Nothing ties the two together: there is no in-flight flag or claim anywhere in wx_app.rs, and no test covers two threads. The ledger has no entry for this; 720 and 660 are about which accounts are sent, not about a race.

The concrete case is wrong because the one-second tick (6518-6536) and undo_send (6007) both run on the UI thread. A tick cannot start a flush in the middle of Undo. The real case needs a flush that some other trigger had already spawned before Undo was pressed. Triggers that can do that: another held message coming due a moment earlier, Send Queued Mail, Go Back Online, a Send with the hold off, or a feedback report. That flush must also take its `now`, after its database open, just past A's moment and inside the few milliseconds Undo spends in save_as_draft.

The window is narrow, but when it hits, the person hears "Taken back", the composer reopens a copy, and the message still goes. That is the answer outbox.rs:386-391 and sending_later.rs:496-501 say must never be given. If they then send the draft, it goes twice. The comments at outbox.rs:386-391 and wx_app.rs:24317-24322 also describe a protection that does not exist. Ok(false) from the send loop can only come after a send has finished, never while one is in progress. So the safety claim is false, not just weak.

It is "should" rather than "nice" because the same missing claim drives lead A. Two overlapping flush passes both send a row the first pass has not deleted yet, and that window is seconds of SMTP time, not milliseconds. One fix closes both.

The proposed fix works. One simplification: there is only one process, so the startup step can clear every claim, with no need for an age test.
verdict.corrected_problem:
A read does not claim a row. The flush (wx_app.rs:24587-24603) runs in an rt.spawn task. It takes `now` and reads the queue only after opening the database, then sends, and deletes the row only after the send (24701), ignoring Ok(false). Undo Send (24298, 24337) treats a true from `DELETE ... WHERE id` as proof it caught the message. But true only means the row was there, not that no flush is holding it. The doc comments at outbox.rs:386-391 and wx_app.rs:24317-24322 say the Ok(false) path catches the send loop. It cannot, because the loop removes a row only after its send finishes.

Real case: the tick and Undo share the UI thread, so the tick itself cannot interleave. Instead, a flush is already in flight from another trigger (another held message due a moment earlier, Send Queued Mail, Go Back Online, a hold-off Send, a feedback report). Undo is pressed just before message A's moment and judges A still held. The flush's `now`, taken after its database open, lands just past the moment and inside Undo's draft save, so the flush reads A. Undo's delete then returns true, "Taken back" is announced and the draft reopens, while the flush sends A.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Add a nullable sending_since column through ensure_column_exists. In the flush, just before each send, claim the row with `UPDATE outbox_queue SET sending_since = ?2 WHERE id = ?1 AND sending_since IS NULL`, and skip the row if nothing changed. That skip also closes lead A's overlapping passes. Make Undo's delete `DELETE FROM outbox_queue WHERE id = ?1 AND sending_since IS NULL`, so it returns false for a claimed row, and leave the Outbox's own cancel_queued as it is. Clear the claim in update_outbox_failure, in the same statement. At startup, clear every claim: there is only one process, so no age check is needed.

Correct the two comments (outbox.rs:386-391, wx_app.rs:24317-24322) so they say the claim is what tells Undo it lost.

Write the red test first: claim a row, then assert delete_outbox_message returns false and the row stays.

An in-process alternative of similar size, with no schema change: an Arc<Mutex<HashSet<id>>> shared by the flush task and Undo. The flush holds the lock while it reads the queue and records the ids. Undo holds it while it checks and deletes.

all.title: Settings are rewritten in place, so a crash mid-write loses every setting
all.location: src/data/config.rs:1188-1222 (fs::write of app_config.json and account_*.json), 1146-1154 (load fails on a partial file); src/presentation/wx_app.rs:15462-15467, 15758-15762, 18292-18296
all.what_this_is: ConfigManager saves the settings file after every change: mute, columns, default account, Settings OK, and the first-run answers.
all.problem: fs::write truncates the file and then writes it, so it is not atomic. Worker threads call load_stored() at any moment, for example the flush at wx_app.rs:24645, and can read the empty file between the truncate and the write. Power loss or a kill during a save leaves an empty or partial JSON file for good.
all.concrete_case: The column layout is saved while the window closes and Windows shuts down, leaving app_config.json at 0 bytes. On the next start every load_stored() fails. Readers fall back to defaults: theme, keep_sent_mail_on_this_computer, per-account allowed changes falling to NOTHING, and the first-run flag. Every setter that begins with load_stored (15462, 15758, 18292, and wx_account_manager.rs:1514, 1564) refuses to save until the person opens Settings and overwrites the file, after which all earlier choices are gone. A flush that reads during a normal save gets keep_sent_mail_on_this_computer = false for that pass.
all.fix: Write to app_config.json.tmp and then fs::rename it over the original, which replaces the file atomically on NTFS. Do the same for the account files. That is about four lines in save_app_config and save.
all.if_skipped: A rare crash at the wrong moment silently resets every setting, including what the program may change at servers.
all.ledger_entry: new

verdict.reason: I checked each claim against the code and found nothing about this in .planning/WINDOWS.md. config.rs:1201 and 1217 save with a plain fs::write, which empties the file and then writes it, with no temporary file, no flush and no rename. config.rs:1150-1154 makes load() fail on an empty or partial file, and the `?` inside the account loop (1170-1177) means one bad account file fails the whole load as well. The settings file is re-read on many worker paths, including allowed_for at allowed.rs:1059, which runs every time a client is built, and the send flush at wx_app.rs:24645. The setters at wx_app.rs 15462, 15758 and 18292, and at wx_account_manager.rs 1514 and 1564, all return without saving when load_stored fails. Only handle_settings (wx_app.rs:22327-22334) opens on defaults and writes over the bad file. Nothing on screen says the settings could not be read; it only goes to the log. The project already writes atomically in mailbox_archive.rs:1097-1106 (sync_all, then rename), so the pattern is a known one here. Two parts of the finding overstate it. A normal Windows shutdown flushes its cache, so a 0-byte file needs a kill in the microsecond gap between emptying and writing. The realistic causes are hard power loss, a crash of Windows itself, or a forced reset within seconds of a save, which leave an empty or zero-filled file. And the first-run question is skipped, not asked again (wx_app.rs:36026-36031). The race between a running save and a read on another thread is real but very short, and it fails safe: that one read sees NOTHING allowed, or keep_sent_mail false. It is rare, but when it hits, every setting resets with no warning, so this is should, not must.
verdict.corrected_problem: save_app_config (config.rs:1201) and the account loop in save (1217) write the file in place with fs::write: it empties the file, then writes it, with no flush. Two cases go wrong. (1) Hard power loss, a crash of Windows itself, or a forced reset within seconds of a save can leave app_config.json empty or full of zero bytes. A normal shutdown does not, because Windows flushes its cache and the process would have to die in the microsecond gap between emptying and writing. (2) Another thread that reads the settings during a save can get an empty file. After case 1, every load_stored() fails from then on. allowed_for (allowed.rs:1059) answers NOTHING for every account, so the program quietly becomes read-only. Theme, columns, mute and keep-sent-mail all read as defaults, and the first-run question is skipped (wx_app.rs:36026), not asked again. The setters that start with load_stored refuse to save. Nothing on screen says the settings are unreadable, only the log. The only way back is opening Settings, which shows defaults and writes over the file, so every earlier choice is gone. Case 2 lasts for one read, and that read fails safe (NOTHING allowed, keep_sent_mail false). The account files only matter where account_*.json files already exist on disk: nothing in src ever adds to account_configs, so save only rewrites files that load found.
verdict.corrected_fix: Add one small helper in config.rs and call it from save_app_config and from the account loop in save. It copies mailbox_archive.rs:1097-1106: write the content to a file beside the target whose name does not end in .json (for example app_config.json.saving), call sync_all on it, then fs::rename it over the target. The rename replaces the old file in one step. If anything fails, delete the temporary file and return the error. sync_all is required: a rename without it can still leave a zero-filled file after power loss on NTFS. The temporary name must not end in .json, or load() at config.rs:1169 would parse a leftover account temporary file as an account. A possible red test: put a directory at the temporary path and assert that save returns an error and leaves the old app_config.json unchanged. Today save ignores that path and succeeds, so the test starts red. Telling the user when the settings are unreadable is a separate, larger change and is not part of this fix.

all.title: A user folder named Deleted, Bin or Trash anywhere in the tree can become the account's Trash, so deletes go there and the unattended emptying expunges it
all.location: src/service/protocols/imap/special_use.rs:18-23 and :75-81; src/service/protocols/imap.rs:889-891; src/data/message_cache/folders.rs:846; src/application/destinations.rs:100-109; src/application/emptying_the_trash.rs:345-363 and :466-482; src/presentation/wx_app.rs:27078-27094
all.what_this_is: Folder roles come from the server's SPECIAL-USE attribute, or else from the folder's last path segment. The account's Trash is then whichever Trash-typed folder `where_a_deleted_message_goes` meets first.
all.problem: The name check runs on folders at any depth, even when another folder carries the server's own `\Trash` attribute. When two folders are typed Trash, the first one wins. Folders are sorted by (kind, lowercased path), saved in that order, and read back `ORDER BY id`, so the alphabetically first Trash-typed folder becomes the Trash.
all.concrete_case: The server lists `(\Trash) "Trash"` and the person's own `() "Clients/Deleted"`. `from_name("Deleted")` types the second one as Trash too (special_use.rs:81). "clients/deleted" sorts before "trash" (imap.rs:889, types.rs:199), so it gets the lower id when the account is added. After that: every Delete in the account moves mail into Clients/Deleted. Delete pressed inside Clients/Deleted becomes DeleteOutright (destinations.rs:106-107, wx_app.rs:27090) and is expunged at the server. With Empty the Trash after 30 days turned on, `empty_at_a_check` picks Clients/Deleted (emptying_the_trash.rs:441). The in_the_trash_since trigger stamped those rows at the first sync, so 30 days later the check starts expunging the person's archived client mail, AT_MOST_IN_A_DAY a day, with nobody at the keyboard.
all.fix: In `classify`, use the name fallback only for a top-level folder or one directly under INBOX. Anything deeper with no attribute is Custom. Gmail's `[Gmail]/...` folders always carry attributes, so the `[Gmail]/Sent Mail` name case at special_use.rs:193 moves to an attribute test.
all.if_skipped: The first person who adds an existing mailbox with an archived Deleted, Bin or Deleted Items folder and turns on emptying loses that folder from the server, and deleting inside it is already permanent.
all.ledger_entry: Not in the ledger. Entries 771 and 784 cover emptying on a real server, not which folder is chosen.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this by reading the code, and the real damage is worse than the finding says. `classify` (special_use.rs:18-23) falls back to the folder's last path segment at any depth, and `from_name` (:81) types bin, deleted, deleted items and deleted messages as Trash. The function looks at one folder at a time, so the server declaring `\Trash` on a different folder does not stop it.

`get_folders_for_account` (folders.rs:844-872) reads `ORDER BY id` and then sorts again by `tree_position(kind, name)`. `name` is the leaf (mail_sync.rs:715, 761, imap.rs:870), so two Trash-typed folders are ordered by leaf name. "bin", "deleted", "deleted items" and "deleted messages" all sort before "trash", whatever their depth. A nested "Trash" ties with the real one and wins on id, because ids follow the insert order from imap.rs:889, which sorts by display path ("imported/trash" before "trash").

`where_a_deleted_message_goes` (destinations.rs:100-107) takes the first Trash-typed folder. Every Delete then moves mail into the person's folder, and a Delete inside that folder becomes DeleteOutright (wx_app.rs:27091). Custom folders the person is subscribed to sync by default (mail_sync.rs:2131-2136). Their rows are stamped by the `a_message_is_put_in_the_trash` trigger when they are inserted (mod.rs:2658-2664), so After 15 or 30 days expunges them at the server (emptying_the_trash.rs:441, 466-482).

The finding understates the "When Wixen Mail closes" choice. `empty_one_imap_trash_on_the_way_out` (:821-846) expunges everything in that folder on the first close, with no wait at all.

Emptying is off by default and only runs for accounts this program empties, not Gmail or Microsoft ones. The wrong folder for Delete, and permanent delete inside it, affect every provider. For example, Microsoft's declared "Deleted Items" loses to a user's "Archive/Deleted". A mailbox migrated into a subfolder such as "Old/Deleted Items" or "Imported/Trash" is a likely way to meet this.

No test covers a nested name beside a declared Trash. `test_only_the_last_segment_of_a_path_is_matched` asserts that nested names match by design. The ledger has nothing on special_use.rs or destinations.rs, and entry 771 covers emptying at a real server, not which folder is chosen. The proposed fix limits the name fallback by depth only. That does not close a top-level user "Bin" or "Deleted" next to a declared "Trash", so the fix below adds a second rule.
verdict.corrected_problem: Folder roles come from SPECIAL-USE attributes, or otherwise from the folder's leaf name at any depth. This happens even when another folder in the same LIST already declares that role. `get_folders_for_account` sorts by (kind, lowercased leaf name), not by id. So among Trash-typed folders, a person's own "Bin", "Deleted", "Deleted Items" or "Deleted Messages", top-level or nested, always comes before the real "Trash". A nested "Trash" ties with it and wins because its id is lower. `where_a_deleted_message_goes` picks that folder. Delete moves mail into it, and Delete inside it is permanent. An emptying schedule expunges its synced archive at the server: after 15 or 30 days, or on the first close with "When Wixen Mail closes".
verdict.corrected_fix:
In `list_folders` (imap.rs, before the map at :852), work out whether any listed mailbox declares a role attribute, and pass that flag to `classify`. When the flag is set, take roles from attributes only and type every other folder as Custom. When it is not set, keep the name fallback, but only for a top-level folder or one directly under INBOX. Update `test_only_the_last_segment_of_a_path_is_matched`: `INBOX.Sent` stays Sent, and `[Gmail]/Sent Mail` with no attributes becomes Custom, because Gmail always declares its folders. Add red tests first:
- `\Trash` "Trash" plus a bare "Clients/Deleted": the second is Custom.
- `\Trash` "Trash" plus a bare top-level "Bin": "Bin" is Custom.
- No attributes at all and a bare "Imported/Trash": it is Custom.

all.title: A rule's move leaves a row the destination never reconciles, so every message a rule files shows twice in the destination
all.location: src/application/mail_sync.rs:1343-1380; src/data/message_cache/messages.rs:912-935, :2113-2117, :2133-2137; compare src/application/moves_waiting.rs:931-962
all.what_this_is: `carry_out_the_moves` sends UID MOVE for each message a rule files, then calls `cache.move_message(row, into.id)`.
all.problem: `cache.move_message` gives the row a reserved number from the top of the range and sets filed_here=1. A manual move later settles that row to the server's real number through `settle_the_row` (`the_server_holds_it_at`). A rule's move never does. Sync skips filed_here rows when it compares (`stored_uids`), and `forget_message` refuses to delete them.
all.concrete_case: A rule moves mail from billing@ into Invoices on an IMAP account. The server answers Moved::Moved, and the row lands in Invoices as uid 4294967295 with filed_here=1. The next read of Invoices (later in the same check, or when the folder is opened) lists the message under the new UID the server assigned. That UID is not in `stored`, so the message is fetched and stored again. Invoices now shows the invoice twice, permanently. The reserved-number row can never be opened either: its text is requested under a number the server never issued, and `fetch_body` fails with "returned no message" (imap.rs:1255).
all.fix: After `Moved::Moved`, settle the row the way the replay does instead of leaving the reserved number: ask `uids_with_message_id(into.path, message_id)`. If there is exactly one answer, call `the_server_holds_it_at(row, into.id, uid)`. Otherwise call `let_the_next_read_bring_it(row)`. That is a few lines in place of the bare `cache.move_message`.
all.if_skipped: Every rule that files mail on an IMAP account doubles the destination folder's contents, and half the rows cannot be opened.
all.ledger_entry: Not in the ledger. Entry 681 is about how carry_out_the_moves counts moves, not about the row it leaves.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this by reading the code line by line. After the server answers Moved::Moved, `carry_out_the_moves` (mail_sync.rs:1343-1380) only calls `cache.move_message`. For a folder on the server, `numbering_in` gives `FiledHereCountingDownFromTheTop` (importing_messages.rs:112-117), so `move_message_from` (messages.rs:910-942) gives the row a reserved number from the top of the range and sets filed_here=1. `Moved::Moved` carries no new UID (imap.rs:286-297), and nothing on this path settles the row afterwards.

On the next read of the destination, `stored_uids` leaves the marked row out (messages.rs:2116), so it also plays no part in `highest_uid`. The server's new UID therefore lands in `uids_to_fetch`, and `upsert_messages` inserts a second row keyed on (folder_id, uid). The upsert does not match by message_id (messages.rs:1257-1265). `forget_message` will not delete a marked row (messages.rs:2136), so the duplicate stays for good. The text fetcher skips it as "the only copy is here" (bodies.rs:668), so it never gets its text either.

The project already knows this shape. The comment on `let_the_next_read_bring_it` (data/message_cache/moves_waiting.rs:499-501) says a row with a number the server never gave "would sit beside the real message once the folder is read". The manual-move replay avoids it through `settle_the_row` (moves_waiting.rs:931-962), but the rule path does not. The test at messages.rs:3209-3251 actually locks in "a real message arrives beside the rule-filed row", treating it as a different message. Ledger 681 is about counting only, and I found no ledger entry about this row.

It is reachable in normal use: any IMAP account with a move_to_folder rule and changes allowed. Every message such a rule files then shows twice in the destination. I did not trace the reader path, so the claim that the reserved-number copy cannot be opened is plausible but unchecked. The duplicate on its own is enough to make this a must.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Make the bound on `carry_out_the_moves` `M: Mailbox + ReplaysAMove`. `sync_folder` already has that bound and already passes the same controller to `carry_out_the_deletes`.

After `Moved::Moved`, keep the `cache.move_message` call and then settle the row the way `settle_the_row` does:

1. Read `cache.get_message(moving.message_row)` to get its message_id.
2. Ask `controller.where_it_is(&into.path, &message.message_id)`. This is the trait method that `MailController::uids_with_message_id` sits behind, and it selects the destination itself. The later flag read selects the source folder again.
3. If there is exactly one `[uid]`, call `cache.the_server_holds_it_at(row, into.id, uid)`. That call already handles the case where the sync brought the message down first.
4. For any other answer, or an error, call `cache.let_the_next_read_bring_it(row)`.

Red test first: run `sync_with_rules` on INBOX with a move_to_folder Invoices rule, with Scripted answering where_it_is with [12] and then listing [12] for Invoices. Sync Invoices and assert it holds exactly one row for the message, unmarked, at uid 12. Also revisit the test at messages.rs:3209, which currently treats the arriving copy as a different message.
verdict.corrected_problem: The row a rule's move leaves in an IMAP destination keeps a reserved number with filed_here=1, and nothing ever settles it to the server's real UID. The manual-move replay does settle its row, in `settle_the_row`. Because sync leaves marked rows out of `stored_uids`, and `forget_message` refuses to delete them, the next read of the destination fetches the moved message under its new UID as a second row. The reserved-number row stays beside it for good, and the text fetcher skips it because it counts as the only copy.

all.title: The text download spins forever when one or two messages always fail to fetch
all.location: src/presentation/wx_app.rs:29957-30100 (the loop, arm at :30061); src/application/mail_sync.rs:2626-2648; src/data/message_cache/bodies.rs:657-669; src/service/protocols/imap.rs:1255-1257; src/application/finding_what_was_deleted.rs:170
all.what_this_is: The download-everything runner repeatedly reads `messages_with_no_text_here`, asks `what_to_do_next`, fetches one chunk, and loops.
all.problem: Nothing records messages that failed. A chunk ends early only after 3 failures in a row. When the only messages still missing text are 1 or 2 that always fail, each chunk 'went through the whole list' and the loop asks for the same messages again, with no wait and no limit.
all.concrete_case: A Dovecot (CONDSTORE) account. Two messages arrive, the check stores their headers, and the person deletes both on their phone. The download starts right after the check (wx_app.rs:30821). Resumed syncs never forget rows, and the next full comparison is up to 6 hours away. Each `UID FETCH n BODY.PEEK[]` answers OK with no data, which fails as "returned no message". That is 2 failures, under 3, so the runner re-reads the same two and asks again, hundreds of times a second, until a check forgets them. A message `mime::parse` cannot read (mail_sync.rs:2676) loops the same way forever. While it spins, `downloading.running` stays true and each turn runs a whole-account `messages_with_no_text_here` query. With 3 or more such messages in a row, the run instead ends with `break 'accounts` (:30097), so every account listed after this one never gets its download, retried on backoff indefinitely.
all.fix: In the text arm, end this account's text pass when a chunk fetched nothing: `Ending::WentThroughTheWholeList if done.fetched == 0 => break`. This is the text-side twin of `stopped_coming_down` for headers. Better still, keep a per-run set of message ids that failed and filter them out of `missing`.
all.if_skipped: The first real account where someone deletes fresh mail on another device pins a CPU core and hammers the provider. Gmail-style rate limits apply to exactly this.
all.ledger_entry: Not in the ledger. Entries 11 and 72 cover whether providers tolerate the chunk sizes, not this loop.

verdict.reason:
I checked each step in the code, and the loop is real.
- In the runner at wx_app.rs:30061, the `Ending::WentThroughTheWholeList` arm logs, reports progress, calls `worked()` (which resets the backoff) and loops. Nothing in it can end the loop.
- `fetch_over_a_mailbox` (mail_sync.rs:2626-2648) only ends a chunk early after 3 failures in a row. A chunk with 1 or 2 failures and no successes still comes back as `WentThroughTheWholeList`.
- `messages_with_no_text_here` (bodies.rs:657-669) skips only rows that have text, deleted rows and only-copy rows. Nothing records that a message failed, so a failed message comes back at the same place, newest first.
- `fetch_body` (imap.rs:1255) turns "OK with no data" into `Error::Protocol`, and a `mime::parse` failure (mail_sync.rs:2676) is counted the same way.

The download does not forget deleted rows either. When every folder's held count is at least `total_on_server`, it never asks for headers again. A check on a CONDSTORE server resumes (`what_to_ask_for`, mail_sync.rs:564-569) and only lists every uid once the 6-hour comparison is due. Every check ends with `DownloadRequested` (wx_app.rs:30821).

So with 1 or 2 messages left that always fail, the runner keeps asking for them with no wait. That lasts until a check forgets them: minutes on Gmail, up to 6 hours on a CONDSTORE server. For a message the server always refuses, or one that cannot be parsed, it never ends.

Two cases the finding misses:
- One message over 16 MiB at the front of the list goes out alone, in a chunk of one (bringing_everything_down.rs:172). If it always fails, the loop spins on it while the rest of the account's text waits.
- Each turn writes 2 warning lines to the log and sends a `Progress` update to the window, which is spoken under "Say every step". That breaks guardrail 5.

The second claim also holds. When 3 or more always-failing messages end up together at the front, the run ends with `break 'accounts` (:30097). Accounts listed after this one never get their download, and the run is retried on the backoff for as long as those messages stay.

This is not in the ledger. Ledger 11 and 72 ask whether providers tolerate the chunk sizes. 524 is about the unused whole-list function.

Two parts of the finding are overstated. "Hundreds of times a second" and "pins a CPU core" are too strong. Each turn makes two round trips to the server plus two queries over the whole account, so it runs tens of times a second over the internet. The fix is still needed.

The finding's main fix, `done.fetched == 0 => break`, stops the spin, but it also stops the account's text download for good behind one bad large message. Leaving out the messages already asked for in this run fixes both, and it is three lines.
verdict.corrected_problem:
Nothing records that a message failed. In the text arm (wx_app.rs:30061) a chunk that went through the whole list always loops. A chunk only ends early after 3 failures in a row (mail_sync.rs:2640). So a chunk of 1 or 2 messages that always fail is asked for again and again, with no wait and with the backoff reset by `worked()`.

This happens in three cases:
- The only messages still missing text are 1 or 2 that always fail. This includes a message deleted on another device. On a CONDSTORE server the row stays for up to 6 hours, because the download does not ask for headers again once each folder's count is complete, and a check only lists every uid once the 6-hour comparison is due. A message the server always refuses, or one `mime::parse` cannot read, keeps it going forever.
- A message over 16 MiB that always fails sits at the front of the list. It goes out alone in a chunk of one, and the rest of the account waits behind it.

Each turn makes two round trips to the server, runs two queries over the whole account, writes two warning lines to the log and sends a progress update to the window. The progress update is spoken under "Say every step".

There is a second problem. Once 3 or more messages that always fail end up together at the front, every run ends with `break 'accounts` (:30097). The accounts listed after this one never get their download, and the run is retried on the backoff for as long as those messages stay.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In `start_the_download`, keep a `HashSet<i64>` of message ids asked for during this account's run, created next to `text_to_fetch`.
1. After `messages_with_no_text_here`, remove those ids from `missing`.
2. In the `TheNextChunkOfText` arm, add `messages.iter().map(|m| m.message_id)` to the set.

Each message is then asked for at most once per run, and the run carries on past a bad message rather than spinning or stopping. That is 3 lines.

The test comes first: a scripted mailbox where one message always fails, with the runner's turn driven through it, and an assertion that it stops.

The finding's `fetched == 0 => break` stops the spin too, but it leaves the account's text download stuck for good behind one large message that fails.

Fixing the other accounts being starved (3 messages that always fail, together at the front) needs one more step. Either keep the set in `s.downloading` for the session, or end only this account's loop on a text-chunk refusal while still setting `AServerStopped` so the backoff happens. That can come after the main fix.

all.title: When more than 500 messages arrive between checks, the overflow skips the rules and the new-mail count
all.what_this_is: A check fetches at most INITIAL_FETCH_LIMIT (500) missing UIDs per folder, newest first, and runs the rules only on what that check stored.
all.problem: Messages that arrived since the last check but fall outside the newest 500 are never seen by a check. On the resume path the next check starts above the new highest UID. The download of everything then brings them in through `sync_folder(..., filtering: None, MoreOfWhatIsAlreadyThere)`, so no rule ever runs on them.
all.concrete_case: The app is closed for a week and 800 messages reach INBOX on a CONDSTORE server. The first check asks `TheUidsAbove(highest)` (mail_sync.rs:567-568). `uids_to_fetch` keeps the newest 500 (:401-403), the rules run on those 500, and the check says "500 new messages". The other 300 come in through the download with no rules. A blocked sender's mail and "move newsletters to Lists" rules are not applied to 300 messages, which stay in INBOX. A server without CONDSTORE behaves the same, because the download runs straight after the check and takes the gap first.
all.fix: In `uids_to_fetch`, when anything is already held, take every missing UID above the highest held one, and apply `limit` only to the older backfill. That is about 4 lines, and the first sync of an empty folder keeps its 500 cap.
all.if_skipped: Rules, including the block-sender rules `blocking.rs` writes, silently fail on exactly the busiest days.
all.ledger_entry: Not in the ledger.

verdict.reason: I traced every step and each one holds. `uids_to_fetch` (mail_sync.rs:389-405) sorts the missing UIDs newest first and cuts them at `limit`, and the check passes INITIAL_FETCH_LIMIT = 500 with the account's rules (wx_app.rs:30667-30675). On the resume path, `what_to_ask_for` returns TheUidsAbove(highest) (:567-568). The check then stores the newest 500, so the next check asks above the new top and never sees the 300 below it. Rules only run on what that call stored (`apply_rules(cache, rules, &arrived)` at :1877-1880). Every check that goes through ends by asking for the download (:30821). `start_the_download` runs unless downloading is paused or still waiting after a refusal. `what_to_do_next` sends a folder with held < total_on_server to TheNextChunkOfHeaders, inbox first (bringing_everything_down.rs:261-269). That chunk calls `sync_folder(..., None, MoreOfWhatIsAlreadyThere)` (wx_app.rs:29995-30008). MoreOfWhatIsAlreadyThere means EveryUid, and the newest missing UIDs are the 300-message gap, so they are stored with no rules. On Gmail (no CONDSTORE) the download takes the gap the same way, straight after the check. The only time rules reach the gap is when downloading is paused and a later full-listing check, either a due full comparison or a non-CONDSTORE check, takes it first. The count is short as well: "Mail check finished. 500 new messages." and WhatArrived only count what the check fetched, and the other 300 arrive as MoreOfTheFolderArrived with nothing said. Block rules are filter rules (blocking.rs:3-8), so blocks miss too. The project treats a rule that silently does nothing as a defect: `apply_rules` logs and counts rules it holds back for exactly that reason. Branch and main have the same mail_sync.rs and wx_app.rs. No test covers more than 500 arrivals above the highest held UID. Nothing in .planning/WINDOWS.md covers it. A common case (back from a week away with a busy inbox) hits it.
verdict.corrected_problem: When more than 500 messages reach one folder between checks, the check stores the newest 500 and runs the rules on those. The UIDs between the old highest held and the oldest of those 500 are skipped. On a resumed folder the next check asks only above the new top. The download that every check starts then fetches the gap newest first through sync_folder(..., None, MoreOfWhatIsAlreadyThere), so no rule ever runs on those messages (moves, deletes, blocks, sounds). The check's "N new messages" line and the WhatArrived sentence also leave them out. The gap reaches the rules only if downloading is paused or waiting and a later full-listing check takes it first.
verdict.corrected_fix: Change only `uids_to_fetch`. Keep the early return when `limit == 0`. When `stored` is non-empty, always take every missing UID above `stored.max()`, and apply `limit` only to the missing UIDs below it. When `stored` is empty, keep the cap of 500 newest. The first commit is a failing unit test: held [1..=10], on server [1..=810], limit 500, expect 11..=810. `fetch_headers` already splits the UID set into server-safe pieces (`sequence_set::chunks`), so a large arrival will not break the server command. The cost is one bigger fetch and one bigger insert. If that is too much for a bulk copy of tens of thousands into a folder, loop the fetch, store and rules steps of `sync_folder` in INITIAL_FETCH_LIMIT batches within the same check rather than bring the cap back.

all.title: One POP message with no readable header block stops that account's mail permanently
all.location: src/application/pop_sync.rs:265-268 and :327; src/service/mime.rs:289-292; compare src/service/protocols/imap.rs:1968
all.what_this_is: POP sync downloads every new message, oldest first, then sends QUIT to commit.
all.problem: `crate::service::mime::parse(&raw)?` returns early on a message mail-parser rejects. mail-parser returns None whenever it finds no headers. The early return also skips `server.finish()`. The same message is first in line on every later check.
all.concrete_case: A POP maildrop holds a message that begins with a blank line, or a zero-length file. RETR succeeds and `MessageParser::parse` returns None, so the sync fails with "The message could not be read". Every later check retrieves the same message first (to_fetch keeps server order, :132-140) and fails again. No message after it is ever downloaded for that account. The IMAP header path treats the same failure as a message with empty fields (`mime::parse(headers).unwrap_or_default()`, imap.rs:1968).
all.fix: Use `mime::parse(&raw).unwrap_or_default()` and, when parsing failed, store `String::from_utf8_lossy(&raw)` as the plain body. The message is then kept, POP's removal policy cannot delete the only copy unread, and the queue moves on.
all.if_skipped: One malformed message from any sender ends mail delivery for that POP account until someone removes it with another client.
all.ledger_entry: Not in the ledger.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by reading the code. At pop_sync.rs:267, `mime::parse(&raw)?` returns before the message is stored, before the removal loop (:313) and before finish() (:327). mime.rs:290-292 turns mail-parser's None into Error::Protocol("The message could not be read"). Because nothing is stored, the UIDL never joins already_have (:261). to_fetch (:132-140) keeps server order, so every later check fails on that message again and nothing after it ever downloads. The controller is created fresh for each check (wx_app.rs:27439), so skipping finish() leaks nothing, and no DELE has been sent at that point. The caller only reports the error, through fail(). No ledger entry exists and no pop_sync test covers it. One part of the concrete case is wrong. In mail-parser 0.11.5, a message that begins with a blank line parses: parse_headers returns true at the first '\n' (header.rs:18-20) and the body part is pushed (message.rs:380), so the result is Some. parse_ returns None only when no header was found and no blank line ended the header block (message.rs:551-567). That happens for a zero-length RETR, where read_data returns no lines and pop3.rs:372-378 builds an empty raw. It also happens for a message in which every line lacks a colon and there is no blank line. "From any sender" is overstated: delivery agents add Return-Path and Received headers, so the realistic trigger is a zero-byte or corrupt message on the server, which is rare. The impact is still total for that account, and it matches a failure the project already fixed once (the UTF-8 comment at pop3.rs:472-476). Hence should, not must.
verdict.corrected_problem: pop_sync::sync propagates a mime::parse failure with `?` (pop_sync.rs:267). The message is never written, so its UIDL never reaches already_have. Every later check retrieves it first, in server order, and fails the same way. No later message downloads, and the removal policy (:309-323) never runs, so on an account set to clear its server the mailbox also stops emptying. The error sentence does not say which message it is. In mail-parser 0.11.5 the failure happens only when no header line was found and no blank line ended the header block. In practice that means a zero-length message on the server (RETR answers with no lines, so raw is empty). A message whose every line lacks a colon and has no blank line does the same. A message beginning with a blank line parses fine. Skipping finish() is harmless in itself: the controller is per check and no DELE has been sent yet.
verdict.corrected_fix: Red first: a pop_sync test using Scripted::holding with a zero-length message followed by an ordinary one. Then at pop_sync.rs:267 use `let parsed = crate::service::mime::parse(&raw).unwrap_or_else(|why| { tracing::warn!("A downloaded message could not be read and is kept as plain text: {why}"); crate::service::mime::ParsedMessage { body_plain: Some(String::from_utf8_lossy(&raw).into_owned()), ..Default::default() } });`. ParsedMessage already derives Default (mime.rs:34). The message is then stored under its UIDL, the queue moves on, and removal applies only to a copy this computer holds. all.title: Each check reads the flags of every held message and makes about six SQL statements per message outside a transaction
all.location: src/application/mail_sync.rs:1946-1999; src/data/message_cache/tags.rs:39-70; src/data/message_cache/folders.rs:764 and :792
all.what_this_is: The flag read-back that brings changes made on other devices down to this computer.
all.problem: With no stored modseq, `fetch_flags` returns every held UID. Each one then gets: `message_row_for_uid`, an autocommit `set_message_flags` UPDATE, `folder_account`, `message_row_for_uid` again, and `match_labels_to_keywords`, which itself reads `get_tags_for_account` and `get_tags_for_message`. None of this is in a transaction, and the account's labels are re-read for every message. `folder_account` and `account_of_folder` are the same query under two names.
all.concrete_case: A server that reports no HIGHESTMODSEQ (the code models Gmail this way, abilities.rs:123-128) and an INBOX of 100,000 messages held after the download. Every schedule tick, watch wake and F9 runs about 600,000 statements for INBOX. Each UPDATE is its own write transaction on the shared WAL database, so the window's own writes (mark read, moves) queue behind them.
all.fix: Wrap the loop in one `unchecked_transaction`, the way `upsert_messages` does. Read the account and its keyword labels once before the loop, and skip label matching when no label has a keyword. Look the row up once per UID. Delete `folder_account` and use `account_of_folder`.
all.if_skipped: Large mailboxes make every check slow and contend with the interface's writes. The cost grows with the mailbox, not with the amount of change.
all.ledger_entry: Entry 70 says every folder is read out in full when CONDSTORE is absent, but nothing records this per-message SQL cost.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed the per-message cost line by line, but the contention claim is wrong and the proposed single transaction would make that part worse.

What holds:
- The modseq is only stored from STATUS's highest_modseq (mail_sync.rs:2000), so a server without CONDSTORE never gets one. `since` stays None and imap.rs:1292-1306 fetches flags for every held UID. `stored` is `stored_uids` (all held, line 1770), and bringing_everything_down.rs makes a fully held mailbox a normal state.
- Each returned UID runs six statements: message_row_for_uid at 1974, set_message_flags at 1986, folder_account at 1991, message_row_for_uid again at 1992, then get_tags_for_account and get_tags_for_message inside match_labels_to_keywords (tags.rs:45-50).
- Three of them are loop-invariant or repeated. The account and the account's labels are re-read per message, and the row is looked up twice. message_row_for_uid, set_message_flags and folder_account use uncached query_row/execute, so each is re-prepared every time.
- There is no transaction anywhere in mail_sync.rs.
- folder_account (folders.rs:764) and account_of_folder (folders.rs:792) run the identical SQL. folder_account's doc comment is also fused with folder_kind's.
- The ledger has no entry for this. Entry 70 is an unrun-verify about whether providers grant CONDSTORE. Entry 695/8981 is about rule flags being overwritten, fixed by 13-44.3. Neither records the local SQL cost.
- The cost is real for servers without CONDSTORE, such as Exchange/Outlook IMAP, and for Gmail as this code models it.

What is wrong:
- "Each UPDATE is its own write transaction, so the window's writes queue behind them" overstates it. With WAL, synchronous=NORMAL and busy_timeout=5000 (mod.rs:1443-1445), an autocommit statement holds the write lock for one indexed UPDATE and then releases it. A no-change UPDATE writes no frames. The interface's writes wait at most one statement, and reads never wait.
- The fix's "wrap the loop in one unchecked_transaction, the way upsert_messages does" is not like upsert_messages. That batch is bounded by the header fetch size. This loop covers every held message, so one transaction would hold the write lock for the whole loop, around a second or more at 100,000 messages. A mark-read on the interface thread would then stall for that long, up to the 5 s busy timeout.

The real harm is CPU time on the sync worker on every check. It grows with the mailbox, and it is probably comparable to the network flag read it follows. It is "should": cheap to fix, but it causes no data loss and does not block the interface.
verdict.corrected_problem:
When the server reports no HIGHESTMODSEQ, every check reads back the flags of every held message. Each one then costs six SQL statements:
- the row lookup (message_row_for_uid, mail_sync.rs:1974)
- the flag UPDATE (1986)
- folder_account (1991)
- the same row lookup again (1992)
- get_tags_for_account and get_tags_for_message inside match_labels_to_keywords (tags.rs:45-50)

The account and its labels are the same for every message in the folder but are re-read for each one. Three of the statements are re-prepared on every call because they use uncached query_row/execute. At 100,000 held messages that is about 600,000 statements per check on the worker thread. The cost grows with the mailbox, not with how much changed.

It does not hold up the interface's writes: each autocommit statement takes the WAL write lock only for itself.

folder_account and account_of_folder (folders.rs:764 and :792) are the same query under two names.
verdict.corrected_fix:
1. Before the loop, read the account and its labels once. This can reuse the account lookup that the_changes_waiting_by_row already makes. Keep only the labels that have a keyword. If none has a keyword, skip label matching entirely.
2. Inside the loop, look the row up once and use it for both the waiting-change lookup and the label match.
3. Give match_labels_to_keywords a form that takes the pre-read keyword labels instead of the account id.
4. Switch message_row_for_uid and set_message_flags to prepare_cached.

That takes a message from six statements to two (three when keyword labels exist), and is about 10 lines.

Do not wrap the whole loop in one transaction. Unlike upsert_messages, whose batch is bounded, this loop covers every held message, so a single transaction would hold the write lock long enough to stall the interface's writes. If a transaction is wanted, commit per chunk of a few hundred, matching the IMAP fetch batches.

Separately, delete folder_account and point its callers at account_of_folder.

all.title: Nothing stops two checks of the same account running at once, so new mail is announced twice and rules run twice
all.location: src/presentation/wx_app.rs:30378-30398, :5180-5186, :6656-6657, :24160-24184, :30780-30784; src/data/message_cache/messages.rs:1265 and :1299; src/application/mail_sync.rs:1871-1880
all.what_this_is: `spawn_mail_sync` is called from F9, start-up, the schedule and the watch.
all.problem: The only guard is `last_checked`, and it only stops the schedule from starting another check. Two workers can sync the same folder at once on the shared session with separate caches. `upsert_message` returns the row id on update as well as on insert, so both workers treat the same message as having just arrived.
all.concrete_case: Start-up runs `check_every_enabled_account`, and the person presses F9 while INBOX is still being read. Both workers read `stored` before either writes, and both fetch UID 101. Both get its row back from `upsert_messages`, both run the rules over it, and both send WhatArrived. The person hears "1 new message" and the new-mail sound twice, plus a rule's sound twice. The watch waking during a check's INBOX pass does the same for one folder.
all.fix: Add a per-account set of checks in flight to WxUIState, checked and set in `spawn_mail_sync`. An account already being checked is skipped and marked 'check again'. When its check finishes, the worker clears the account and starts one more check if the mark is set.
all.if_skipped: Doubled announcements break guardrail 5 (bounded feedback) at the moments people check most often, and rules with side effects run twice.
all.ledger_entry: Not in the ledger.

verdict.reason:
I read every line the finding cites and the case holds. `spawn_mail_sync` (wx_app.rs:30378) has one guard, `last_checked` at :30392-30398, and only `which_are_due` reads it (:27687), so it only holds back the schedule. Four callers start a worker with no guard: F9 (:5186), start-up (:6657), the schedule (:27698) and the watch waking (:24179). Nothing in WxUIState or anywhere in src tracks a check in flight. The download runner does have such a guard (`downloading.running`); checks do not.

Both workers get the same `Arc<MailController>` from `the_session_at` (mail_session.rs:127-151). The session lock is taken per command (mail_controller.rs:445 plus the macro), and tokio's Mutex serves waiters in order. So two workers that start close together take turns command by command. In `sync_folder`, `stored` is read at mail_sync.rs:1770, and `upsert_messages` only writes at :1871, after the SEARCH, the abilities lock and the FETCH. Worker B's STATUS and SELECT fit between A's commands, so B reads `stored` before A writes and both fetch the same UIDs.

Then both workers count the same mail:
- `fetched: fetched.len()` (:2029) counts the server's answer, so both report it as new.
- `upsert_message`'s `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ... RETURNING id` (messages.rs:1265-1299) hands the row back on update too, and `upsert_messages` (:1976) collects those ids. Both run `apply_rules` over the same rows (:1878).
- Both send `WhatArrived` (wx_app.rs:30780). That arm (:23218) signals NewMail and RuleMatched and announces every time, with no de-duplication.

The overlap is easy to hit:
- At start-up, F9 pressed during the sign-in waits on the per-account sign-in lock. Both workers then run side by side from the first folder.
- F9 pressed twice in a row does the same.
- The start-up line "checking N accounts" is a step, which is silent at the default level, so nobody hears that a check is already running.

Not in .planning/WINDOWS.md: I searched for spawn_mail_sync, last_checked, said/heard/run twice, race and watch-waking-during-a-check. Ledger 688 is a different race, between marks and moves.

The proposed fix works but is fragile. The account is cleared in the worker, and the worker leaves an account by about eight `continue` paths and one early return. Missing one blocks that account for the rest of the session. The corrected fix below is smaller: a scoped lock releases itself on every path, and nothing has to remember a "check again" mark.
verdict.corrected_problem: Nothing stops two checks of the same IMAP account at once. Only the schedule reads `last_checked`. F9, start-up and the watch each start a worker regardless. The two workers share one session, which is locked per command and not per check, so they take turns command by command. Worker B can read `stored_uids` for INBOX (mail_sync.rs:1770) after A has read it and before A's `upsert_messages` (:1871). Both then fetch the same UIDs and report them as fetched (:2029). Both get the rows back from the upsert, which returns ids on update (messages.rs:1299), so both run the rules over them. Both send WhatArrived (wx_app.rs:30780), and the arm at :23218 signals NewMail and RuleMatched and announces each time. The easiest way in is F9 pressed during the start-up check's sign-in, or F9 pressed twice. The start-up line saying a check has begun is a silent step at the default level, so the person cannot tell a check is already running.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Run one check per account at a time. Put a per-account lock map in application::mail_session, beside `the_sessions_being_held`. In `spawn_mail_sync`'s worker, take the account's lock (`handle.block_on(lock.lock_owned())`) at the top of each account's pass, before `the_session_at`, and keep the guard until the pass ends. The guard releases itself on every `continue` and return. A second check of the same account then waits for the first, reads `stored` after the first has written it, finds nothing new, and says nothing, because `what_arrived` gives None when nothing arrived. A watch-woken read that comes in during a check still runs after it, so no mail is missed.

Every caller passes accounts in list order and nothing else nests inside this lock, so it cannot deadlock. Crossings use the other account's session and not its check lock.

Red test first: two passes through the locked helper against a scripted server holding one new UID. Assert that the second pass reports fetched 0 and an empty `arrived`.

all.title: A stranger's deeply nested HTML overflows the UI thread's stack and kills the whole program
all.location: src/application/hidden_text.rs:308-348 (Findings::walk recursion); src/vendor/paperback/html_to_text.rs:282-319 and 553-555 (process_node / process_element_children recursion); reached from src/presentation/wx_app.rs:23080-23091 (UIUpdate::MessageBodyLoaded, UI thread) -> the_preview_of 22771 -> reader_text::preview_html 1016-1035 -> body_text 240 and HtmlRenderer::sanitize_and_count_held_back html_renderer.rs:599-605
all.what_this_is: Two walkers over the sender's parsed HTML, one dropping hidden blocks and one turning the body into navigable text. Both recurse once per nesting level, and both run on the main thread every time a message is previewed.
all.problem: Neither walker has a depth bound. html5ever puts no cap on nesting either, unlike Blink's 512. The main thread has the default 1 MB Windows stack, and nothing in build.rs or Cargo.toml raises it. A stack overflow is not a panic: the process aborts, so nothing catches it. No test feeds either walker deep markup.
all.concrete_case: Someone sends an email whose HTML body is `"<div>".repeat(20000) + "hi"`, about 100 KB. The person arrows onto it in the message list. MessageBodyLoaded calls the_preview_of on the UI thread. HtmlToText::convert recurses 20,000 times (two frames per level), and so does hidden_text's walk. The stack overflows and Wixen Mail disappears with no crash log entry. It happens again every time that message is selected, so a screen reader user who keeps arrowing through the inbox keeps crashing until they delete the message somewhere else.
all.fix: Pass a depth argument to both recursions and stop descending past 512, which is the limit browsers already apply: `fn walk(&mut self, node, depth: usize) { if depth > 512 { return; } ... self.walk(child, depth + 1) }`. Do the same in process_node and process_element_children. Add one test per walker that feeds 50,000 nested divs and expects a normal return.
all.if_skipped: Any sender can crash the client remotely, once per selection, with a message that passes every filter.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed it by reading the code. Findings::walk (hidden_text.rs:308-348) and process_node/process_element_children (html_to_text.rs:282-319, 553-555) recurse once per nesting level and have no depth argument. html5ever 0.39.0 has no nesting cap: a search of its tree_builder for depth, MAX or limit finds nothing. Nothing in Cargo.toml, build.rs, .cargo or src sets /STACK or stack_size, so the UI thread has the default 1 MB Windows stack. The chain in the finding is accurate line by line: MessageBodyLoaded (wx_app.rs:23080) calls the_preview_of (22771), which calls preview_html (reader_text.rs:1016). That runs conversation() (1411), which calls body_text (240) and so HtmlToText::convert (html_to_text.rs:176-178). It also runs render_thread_under_a_bar, which calls sanitize_and_count_held_back (html_renderer.rs:1083, 599-605) and so drop_what_the_sender_hid, which calls walk. No test feeds any walker deep markup, and .planning/WINDOWS.md has no entry for this. ammonia is not a problem: its clean_dom uses an explicit stack and its rcdom Drop is iterative.

The finding understates the problem, though, so the proposed fix would not stop the crash:
(1) html_to_text.rs:674-682 collect_text_into is a third recursion. handle_heading, handle_list_item and the title handling call it on the whole subtree. So `<h1>` or `<li>` wrapping 20,000 divs still overflows even with process_node capped.
(2) table_text.rs collect_cell_text, collect_rows and collect_cells recurse over cell contents without a bound.
(3) For an HTML-only body, the crash comes earlier, on a worker. save_message_body calls snippet_of (bodies.rs:319-330, 423), which calls long_text::pieces_of_markup and then read_markup. read_markup runs drop_what_the_sender_hid, then the recursive markup::blocks / blocks_or_a_paragraph walk (long_text.rs:657-674, 736, 991-998). index_message_for_search (searching.rs:365) does the same through words_of_markup. A stack overflow on any thread aborts the whole process, so capping only the two named walkers leaves the remote crash in place.
verdict.corrected_problem: Every walker that turns a stranger's HTML into text recurses once per nesting level with no bound, and html5ever does not limit nesting. The walkers are hidden_text::Findings::walk, HtmlToText::process_node and process_element_children, HtmlToText::collect_text_into (reached through h1-h6, li, title and figcaption), table_text's collect_cell_text, collect_rows and collect_cells, and long_text::markup::blocks and its helpers. A message body like `"<div>".repeat(20000) + "hi"` therefore overflows a stack. An HTML-only body overflows on the worker when it is saved, through snippet_of and then read_markup, or through the search index's words_of_markup. A multipart body overflows on the 1 MB UI thread when it is previewed. A stack overflow aborts the process on any thread, catch_unwind cannot stop it, and it happens again every time the message is opened or fetched. No test covers deep markup, and the ledger has no entry for it.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Put one depth check where the sender's markup is parsed, not a cap in each walker. The two named walkers are not the only ones, and the others would still overflow. Write a small helper, `fn nests_deeper_than(root: NodeRef<Node>, limit: usize) -> bool`. It walks `root.traverse()` without recursion, counts Edge::Open and Edge::Close, and returns true as soon as the depth passes 512. Call it right after the scraper parse in the three entry points:
- In hidden_text::drop_what_the_sender_hid, when the markup is too deep, return `(html.to_string(), 0)`. ammonia and WebView2 already handle deep trees: ammonia does not recurse, and Chromium caps nesting at 512.
- In HtmlToText::convert, return false. body_text already falls back to showing the text when convert fails.
- In long_text::read_markup, fall back to the text nodes gathered with `.descendants()`.
table_text parses subtrees serialized from a document that has already passed the check, so it inherits the bound. Add red tests that feed 50,000 nested divs, plus one variant wrapped in `<h1>`, through body_text/preview_html and through save_message_body with an HTML-only body, and expect a normal return. Before settling on 512, confirm it in a debug build on a 1 MB stack.

all.title: An OAuth token for the whole mailbox is sent to whatever IMAP or SMTP host the account names
all.location: src/application/who_runs_the_mail.rs:15-26 and 90-95 (provider falls back to the address, and the outgoing server is never read); src/application/mail_auth.rs:94-123; src/service/protocols/imap.rs:629-640 (AUTHENTICATE XOAUTH2 to config.server, no host check); src/service/protocols/smtp.rs:626-629; src/presentation/wx_app.rs:24674 (flush_outbox)
all.what_this_is: How the client decides to sign in with a Google or Microsoft token, and which server receives that token.
all.problem: The provider is taken from the incoming server, then the address, then the saved name. The token is then handed to the configured IMAP, POP or SMTP host with no check that the host belongs to the provider that issued it. A Gmail token carries https://mail.google.com/ (oauth.rs:95), which is full read, delete and send access. Any server that advertises AUTH=XOAUTH2 receives a bearer token it can replay for an hour. Thunderbird gates OAuth on the hostname for exactly this reason.
all.concrete_case: Case 1: the account is me@gmail.com with browser sign-in, and the IMAP server was typed as imap.gmial.com. by_the_address answers Gmail, for_account fetches a Google token, and imap.rs:631-640 sends `user=me@gmail.com\x01auth=Bearer ya29...` to imap.gmial.com, which can hold a valid TLS certificate. Case 2: IMAP is imap.gmail.com and SMTP is a non-Google relay. who_runs_the_mail.rs:24 never reads the outgoing server, so flush_outbox hands the same token to that relay as soon as it advertises XOAUTH2.
all.fix: Before using MailAuth::OAuth2, require the destination host to belong to the provider. Expose `by_the_server(host)` and, at the IMAP connect (mail_controller.rs:526, mail_session.rs:714) and the SMTP send (wx_app.rs:24674), refuse with a sentence when `by_the_server(server) != Some(provider)`. Keep the address fallback only for naming the keychain entry.
all.if_skipped: A typo or a hostile server collects a token that gives full control of someone's Gmail or Outlook mailbox.

verdict.reason:
I traced it through the code and it holds. who_runs_the_mail.rs:90-95 picks the provider from the incoming server first, then the address (by_the_address), then the saved name. Nothing ever reads smtp_server; lines 24-27 say so and a test at 331 checks it. mail_auth.rs:94-123 fetches the token for that provider and never compares it with any host. Account::validate (account.rs:236-274) checks no host either. The IMAP path runs sign_in_for (mail_controller.rs:526), then connect_imap(account.imap_server), then imap.rs:629-640, where the XOAuth2 authenticator hands over the bearer credential at the first "+" challenge. A hostile server needs nothing more than that "+". The SMTP path runs from_queued (mail_controller.rs:185, server: account.smtp_server), then smtp.rs:626-629 with mechanism Xoauth2. lettre only sends the token if the relay advertises XOAUTH2, but a hostile relay can advertise it. So both cases work as described. For example: me@gmail.com, browser sign-in ticked, IMAP set to imap.gmial.com. The server check returns None, the address says Gmail, and the token goes to imap.gmial.com. The Google token covers https://mail.google.com/ plus contacts, calendar and tasks (oauth.rs:94-106).

Why should and not must: the user's own settings have to point at the bad host. There is no autoconfig and no account import (searched). The editor fills imap/smtp.gmail.com from the address, and Gmail's browser sign-in is off by default. Also, the risk is already written down. 13-44.5-PLAN.md:1079 lists it as T-13-PK-02, "a token sent to a server the person typed that is not the provider's", medium, disposition accept, for the reason "unchanged". That was a scope decision for that plan, not a judgement that the risk is fine, and it is not open in WINDOWS.md (searched). The fix is cheap, and Thunderbird gates OAuth on the hostname for this reason. No legitimate setup breaks: a custom hostname in front of Google or Microsoft would already fail TLS name checking.

Parts of the finding are wrong. mail_session.rs:714 is inside a #[tokio::test]. POP never receives a token, because wx_app.rs:27424-27435 refuses OAuth2 for POP. The fix it proposes guards three call sites and misses two others that also send the token: the inbox watch (wx_app.rs:27899-27915, watch_folder to account.imap_server) and read receipts (wx_app.rs:27281-27295, SmtpConfig to account.smtp_server).
verdict.corrected_problem: The provider for a browser sign-in falls back from the incoming server to the address and then the saved name, and nothing checks the host before the token is sent. A Google or Microsoft access token therefore reaches any IMAP or SMTP host the account names. Four live paths do this: sign_in_for (mail_controller.rs:526), the inbox watch (wx_app.rs:27899), the outbox flush (wx_app.rs:24674 to from_queued's smtp_server) and read receipts (wx_app.rs:27281). The outgoing server is never read (who_runs_the_mail.rs:24). So an IMAP host that is a typo of Gmail's, or a non-Google SMTP relay on a Gmail account, receives the bearer token if it answers AUTHENTICATE XOAUTH2 or advertises AUTH XOAUTH2. POP is not affected: wx_app.rs:27429 refuses OAuth for POP. The risk is recorded as accepted only as T-13-PK-02 in 13-44.5-PLAN.md, not in the ledger.
verdict.corrected_fix: Add one check in mail_auth::for_account, after provider_of and before credentials_for or get_valid_token, so every caller is covered at once and no token is refreshed for a refused account. When use_oauth is on, refuse with a sentence that names the server to check, unless the incoming server (by protocol) and smtp_server are both the provider's. To do that, make by_the_server pub(crate), or add WhoRunsTheMail::runs(host) -> bool, and compare its answer with WhoRunsTheMail::of(account). Leave provider_of as it is, so the keychain entry name does not change. Write two failing rows in mail_auth's tests first: me@gmail.com with imap_server "imap.gmial.com", and imap.gmail.com with smtp_server "smtp.example.net". Both should return Err without touching the keychain. About 12 lines of code and two tests. Then update T-13-PK-02 in the threat register to mitigate.

all.title: Reply and Forward fetch the sender's remote pictures and tracking pixels, which the reader always holds back
all.location: src/presentation/editor_document.rs:105-113 (HtmlRenderer::new().sanitize_html, which only cleans, html_renderer.rs:570-580); src/presentation/wx_compose.rs:286-305 (without_carried_pictures removes only data: pictures, pictures.rs:251-273) and 1432-1436 (set_page into the live editor WebView); no Content-Security-Policy anywhere in src
all.what_this_is: The reply and forward editor is a live WebView2 page holding the quoted original.
all.problem: The reading path runs hold_back_what_would_be_fetched. That holds back every picture when the Reading switch is off, and holds back tracking pixels even when it is on (pictures.rs:659-666, html_renderer.rs:706-709). The editor runs only the cleaner, so every remote `` in the quoted original is fetched the moment the composer opens.
all.concrete_case: With default settings, a newsletter carries ``. Reading it fetches nothing, because the pixel is held back as a beacon. Pressing Ctrl+R calls quoted_under with ThePictures::StayBehind, which keeps the remote img, and the editor loads it, so the sender learns the message was opened. With pictures blocked in Settings, every remote picture in the original is fetched as well.
all.fix: Add `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="img-src data: cid:">` to the editor document's head in editor_document(). Pictures carried in the body are data: URIs, so they still show. The markup goes out unchanged, so a forward still sends the original's references.
all.if_skipped: Every reply or forward confirms to trackers that the message was opened, which the product promises not to do.

verdict.reason: Confirmed line by line. The reply quotes `s.message_preview`, which is the body exactly as it arrived (wx_app.rs:23087), and that body still holds remote `` addresses, because only `cid:` parts are inlined (pictures.rs:178-200). Reply and Reply All go through `format_reply_body` and then `quoted_under(.., StayBehind)` (wx_compose.rs:271, 286-305). There `without_carried_pictures` replaces only pictures that `is_a_picture_we_carried`, which means our own `data:` ones (pictures.rs:251-273), so `https://` img tags survive. `editor_document` (editor_document.rs:105-113) runs only `sanitize_html`, which is `cleaner().clean()` with nothing held back, and its own comment says so (html_renderer.rs:575-579).
